lesson_title: One Large Pizza or Two Small Ones?
hook_text: A 30 centimetre pizza or two 15 centimetre pizzas for the same price. Most people pick wrong, and the circle formula says why.
clip_script: Same price: one 30 centimetre pizza or two 15 centimetre pizzas. Which is more food? The area of a circle is pi times the radius squared. The big pizza has radius 15, so pi times 225, about 707 square centimetres. The small pizza has radius 7.5, so pi times 56.25, about 177 square centimetres. Two small ones: about 354. The big one is not two small pizzas, it is FOUR, because when you double the radius the squared part becomes four times bigger. That squared is also where the classic mistake lives: a 20 centimetre plate has a radius of 10, so its area is pi times 100, about 314. Square the 20 by mistake and you get about 1257, four times too much. Radius first, always. And half a pie? Half the area, but the edge includes the straight cut as well as the curved crust. Say it: radius first, then square it.
visual_style: Two pizzas side by side on a whiteboard, the small one copied four times to tile the big one exactly; the formula pi r squared writes itself with the radius glowing; a 20 centimetre plate shows the wrong 1257 struck through and the right 314.
pacing: Question posed fast, the two areas at speaking pace, the four-pizzas reveal with a beat, the plate mistake fast, the closing line slow.
